bookTitle: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)

facts.topic: Exchange-Traded Futures vs. OTC Forward Contracts
facts.statement: Futures contracts are standardized agreements traded on public exchanges featuring fixed contract sizes, delivery dates, daily margin settlement, and exchange clearing houses that eliminate counterparty credit risk. In contrast, forward contracts are customized agreements negotiated privately in the over-the-counter (OTC) market with terms tailored to specific counterparties and single settlement at maturity.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Futures Contracts: Standardized contracts traded on public, organized exchanges... clearing houses that eliminate counterparty credit risk [4-6]. Forward Contracts: Non-standardized, customized agreements negotiated directly between two parties in the OTC market [5, 7, 8].

facts.statement: A long position is taken by the trader who agrees to buy the underlying asset at a specified future date and price, whereas a short position is taken by the trader who agrees to sell the underlying asset at a specified future date and price.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Long Position: The position of the trader who agrees to buy the underlying asset at a future date [19]. Short Position: The position of the trader who agrees to sell the underlying asset at a future date [19].

facts.topic: Terminal Payoff Formulas for Long and Short Futures/Forwards
facts.statement: At contract maturity (T), the payoff for a long forward or futures position is equal to the terminal spot price minus the agreed delivery price (S_T - K), while the payoff for a short position is equal to the delivery price minus the terminal spot price (K - S_T).

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Long Position Payoff: Payoff = S_T - K [12, 19]. Short Position Payoff: Payoff = K - S_T [12, 22].

facts.topic: Leverage Ratio and Equity Capital Wipeout Threshold (Lehman Model)
facts.statement: A firm's equity capital percentage equals the reciprocal of its leverage ratio (1 / Leverage Ratio). At Lehman Brothers' 31:1 leverage ratio in 2007, equity capital represented approximately 3.23% of total assets, meaning a mere 3% to 4% decline in asset values completely wiped out its entire equity base.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Equity Capital % = 1 / 31 ≈ 3.23% [23]. A decline of 3–4% in the value of the firm's assets completely wipes out its equity capital base, causing financial collapse [23].

facts.topic: Business Snapshot 1.1: The Lehman Brothers Bankruptcy (September 15, 2008)
facts.statement: On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history, driven by an extreme 31:1 leverage ratio, an aggressive deal-making culture under CEO Dick Fuld that marginalized risk management (removing the Chief Risk Officer in 2007), heavy exposure to subprime assets funded by short-term wholesale debt, and complex entanglement across over 1 million OTC derivative transactions with 8,000 counterparties involving re-hypothecated collateral.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.chapter: ch01_part1 - 4. Real-World Business Snapshots & Case Studies
sourceCitation.excerpt: Lehman had over 1 million outstanding OTC derivative transactions across 8,000 counterparties [27]. Counterparty collateral re-hypothecation led to years of complex litigation over asset ownership [27].

numericalDetails.context: Lehman Brothers September 15, 2008 bankruptcy drivers and OTC contract entanglement

facts.topic: Business Snapshot 1.2: Systemic Risk and Post-2008 CCP Regulations
facts.statement: Systemic risk represents the risk that a default by one financial institution triggers a cascading domino effect of failures across interconnected firms (Bank A defaults, causing massive losses and failure at Bank B, which destabilizes Bank C). To mitigate systemic risk post-2008, regulators mandated Central Counterparties (CCPs) for OTC derivatives, requiring initial margins, daily variation margins, and guaranty funds.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.chapter: ch01_part1 - 4. Real-World Business Snapshots & Case Studies
sourceCitation.excerpt: Systemic Risk: The risk that a default by one financial institution will trigger a domino effect of failures across other financial institutions [20]. Regulatory Remedy: Mandating Central Counterparties (CCPs)... to absorb defaults via initial margin, daily variation margin, and guaranty funds [15, 21, 30].

facts.topic: Global Derivatives Market Sizes (BIS Estimates, Dec 2014)
facts.statement: According to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) as of December 2014, the Over-the-Counter (OTC) derivatives market had $630 trillion in notional principal outstanding and $21 trillion in gross market value, greatly exceeding the $65 trillion underlying asset value traded across organized exchanges.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: OTC Derivatives Notional Principal Outstanding: $630 trillion [29]. OTC Derivatives Gross Market Value: $21 trillion [8]. Exchange-Traded Derivatives Underlying Value: $65 trillion [29].

facts.topic: USD/GBP FX Spot/Forward Quotes and Corporate Hedging (ImportCo & ExportCo)
facts.statement: On May 13, 2015, institutional USD/GBP quotes were Spot 1.5746 Bid / 1.5750 Offer and 3-Month Forward 1.5736 Bid / 1.5742 Offer. Using 3-month forwards, U.S. ImportCo hedges a £10 million payable by buying GBP at the 1.5742 offer rate to lock in a $15,742,000 payment, while U.S. ExportCo hedges a £30 million receivable by selling GBP at the 1.5736 bid rate to lock in $47,208,000 in receipts.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.chapter: ch01_part1 - 5. Numerical Data & Market Statistics & 6. Author Analogies
sourceCitation.excerpt: ImportCo (U.S.): Owes £10 million in 3 months; buys 3-month forward GBP at 1.5742, locking in a payment of $15,742,000 [37, 38]. ExportCo (U.S.): Receives £30 million in 3 months; sells 3-month forward GBP at 1.5736, locking in receipts of $47,208,000 [22, 38].

facts.topic: CME Corn Futures Contract Specifications and Farmer-Merchant Origin
facts.statement: A standard CME Corn futures contract covers 5,000 bushels. At a price quote of 400 cents ($4.00) per bushel, the total contract notional value is $20,000. Historically, this risk-fixing mechanism evolved from June agreements between corn farmers (fearing harvest oversupply price crashes) and food processing firms (fearing scarcity price spikes) to lock in September delivery prices.

generalAssumptions: In institutional foreign exchange interbank markets, market makers quote two-sided Bid and Offer prices where clients buy foreign currency at the higher Offer rate and sell foreign currency at the lower Bid rate.

Exchange-traded futures utilize exchange clearing houses that interpose themselves as counterparties and enforce daily mark-to-market margining, effectively eliminating bilateral counterparty default risk.
Terminal payoff formulas (S_T - K for long, K - S_T for short) evaluate contract value at maturity assuming zero upfront premium payment.
High balance-sheet leverage paired with short-term wholesale debt funding renders financial institutions highly vulnerable to liquidity freezes when asset collateral confidence declines.
Most futures market participants do not take physical delivery of commodities; instead, they close out positions prior to maturity through offsetting trades.
